scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The pogo emerged around 1976 during the early days of London's punk scene.

Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious claimed to have invented the dance to mock non-punk attendees, while others attribute it to his leather poncho restricting movement or his frantic jumping while playing saxophone.
It served as an anti-disco movement to counter mainstream rhythm.
on_screen: Map: United Kingdom · Europe

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed during live music performances of aggressive genres like punk and heavy metal.
It serves as an expression of underground counter-culture, anti-establishment sentiment, and raw energy, underpinned by an unwritten code of community solidarity and safety for fallen dancers.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers jump up and down while either remaining on the spot or moving around.
The classic version involves keeping the torso stiff, arms rigid at the sides, and legs close together like a pogo stick.
Variations allow for thrashing torsos, flailing arms, kicking legs, spinning in the air, and horizontal pushing.
Watch for Up-and-down.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols is widely credited with inventing or popularizing the dance.
Other early figures associated with its lore include Shane MacGowan, Viv Albertine, and Glen Matlock.

Variants include slam dancing (slamming into others), moshing (pushing in a crowd without high vertical jumps), stage diving, slamming from the stage, wall of death (two halves of a crowd crashing together), and circle pits (running in a circle).
The pogo is a direct precursor to modern moshing and slam dancing, sharing historical proximity with ska skanking and rockabilly traditions.
